Wat Khunaram, on Route 4169 in Na Mueang in the south of Koh Samui, displays the body of Luang Pho Daeng, a revered meditation master who died in 1973 while seated in meditation. His body sits upright in a glass case in its own hall. Entry is free, the temple is open in daylight hours, and a visit takes 20–30 minutes. It is an active temple: cover shoulders and knees, keep your voice low and photograph respectfully.

Map and directions

The temple stands right on Route 4169, the island's ring road, in the Na Mueang subdistrict. Driving south from Lamai, pass Hua Thanon and continue west for a few kilometres; the temple is on the roadside before the turn-off to the Na Muang waterfalls. Coming from Nathon, it is on your left after the waterfall junction.

Get directions: open Wat Khunaram in Google Maps.

Who was Luang Pho Daeng?

Luang Pho Daeng (Luang Pho means "Venerable Father") was born on Koh Samui in 1894. He was briefly ordained as a young man in his twenties, but left the monkhood, married and raised six children. He also ran a business and was known locally for helping people in need. Around 1944, at about the age of 50 and with his children grown, he was ordained again and stayed a monk for the rest of his life.

He became a respected teacher of meditation (samatha and vipassana) and served at Wat Khunaram, near where he grew up. He was known for long fasts, and followers say he could go many days without food or water. In 1973, shortly after his 79th birthday, he told those around him that he expected to die soon. He asked that if his body did not decay, it should be placed upright in a glass case as a reminder of the Buddha's teaching that all things are impermanent. He died seated in meditation, and his wish was carried out.

The sunglasses. Over time the eyes sank and decayed, while much of the rest of the body stayed remarkably intact. The monks covered the eye sockets with a pair of sunglasses, partly so that visiting children would not be frightened. This detail made the monk famous with visitors far beyond Samui. Whether he wears them at the time of your visit varies, because the case and robes are tended from time to time. [check]

Good to know: another monk often called Luang Pho Daeng is linked to the seafront chedi at Laem Sor. The names are similar, but they are different people.

Why a monk's body is on display

To many visitors the glass case looks macabre. To Thai Buddhists it is a teaching. Theravada Buddhism, the tradition followed in Thailand, asks people to reflect on three marks of existence: impermanence (anicca), suffering or unsatisfactoriness (dukkha) and non-self (anatta). Contemplating death and the body (maranasati) is a long-standing meditation practice, and forest monks have traditionally meditated on decay as a way to loosen attachment.

By asking for his body to be shown, Luang Pho Daeng turned his own death into a lesson: the body changes and passes, so what matters is how you live and train the mind. For local families the hall is also a place to pay respect to a teacher, ask for blessings and make merit. Seeing it in that light makes the visit feel less like a curiosity and more like what it is for islanders, a visit to a revered elder.

What you'll see, step by step

  1. 1. The temple grounds. From the car park you walk into a typical working temple: traditional buildings, statues, a garden and usually local people praying or making merit.
  2. 2. The display hall. Luang Pho Daeng sits in the glass case at the centre, in the meditation posture he held at the end, wearing saffron robes. Thai visitors kneel, bow three times and leave offerings before they look closely.
  3. 3. Offerings. Flowers, candles, incense and small sheets of gold leaf are sold by the hall for a few dozen baht. You don't have to buy anything, but a small donation in the box is a polite way to say thank you.
  4. 4. A quiet moment. Thai visitors often sit for a minute or two in front of the case before leaving. Read his story (above) before you go in; the visit means more once you know who he was and why he asked to be shown this way.

Visiting respectfully

This is not a museum exhibit but the body of a teacher many islanders still revere. Behave as you would at a funeral or a church service.

  • Cover shoulders and knees. Sarongs are sometimes available on site, but bring your own.
  • Take off your shoes if the hall floor is marked as a shoes-off area, and before any room with a Buddha image.
  • Keep your voice low and switch your phone to silent.
  • Photos: respectful photos are generally allowed. Follow any signs, never use flash, and don't take selfies or pose next to the case.
  • Don't touch the glass or lean on the case.
  • Kneel or sit with your feet tucked away from the monk and from Buddha images.
  • Women should not touch monks or hand them items directly.

Our Koh Samui temples guide covers etiquette at every temple on the island, and Thai culture and traditions explains merit-making.

Is it suitable for children?

It depends on the child. The body is clearly visible and some children find it upsetting; others are fascinated. Explain beforehand what they will see and why the monk asked to be shown this way. The visit is short and you can wait outside with anyone who prefers not to go in.

Best time to visit

Go early in the morning. Coaches and jungle-safari trucks travelling around the ring road usually arrive from late morning, and the hall is small. The temple is open all year. In the north-east monsoon (October to December, with November the wettest month at about 445 mm of rain) it makes a good short stop between showers, since you are under a roof most of the time. February to April is the driest period for combining it with the waterfalls.

Parking and facilities

  • Parking: a roadside car park directly in front of the temple; no fee on normal days. [check]
  • Facilities: basic toilets and drinks stalls; small shops nearby on the ring road.
  • Traffic: Route 4169 is busy and fast here. Take care pulling out on a scooter, especially with traffic coming round the bends.

Grab cars are fewer in the south than in Chaweng, so booking a return can take a while; ask your driver to wait or come with your own transport. Taxis don't use meters, so agree the price first. Songthaews pass on the ring road during the day (locals pay about 30–80 THB). Riding yourself, you need an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category and a helmet (fine up to 2,000 THB). More in getting around Koh Samui.

On a tour: Wat Khunaram is a standard stop on shared 4x4 jungle safaris, together with Na Muang waterfall, the Secret Buddha Garden, Hin Ta and Hin Yai and Big Buddha (market price about 1,700 THB, about 7 hours with lunch). Enquire through our Koh Samui jungle safari page.

Add a boat trip from the south

Thong Krut pier, where the Pig Island boats leave, is about 20 minutes' drive from Wat Khunaram, so the south makes an easy day: temple in the morning, boat in the afternoon. Ang Thong Marine Park is closed from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December.
